elements.text: Ingestion of large birds into both engines
Almost total loss of thrust in both engines
Subsequent ditching on the Hudson River
FAA approval of ditching certification without determining if pilots could attain parameters without engine thrust
Lack of industry flight crew training and guidance on ditching techniques
Captain's difficulty maintaining intended airspeed due to task saturation
Decision-making of flight crewmembers and crew resource management
Fortuitous use of an airplane equipped for extended overwater flight (forward slide/rafts)
Performance of cabin crewmembers expediting evacuation
Proximity and immediate response of emergency responders
Flight and cabin crewmembers were properly certificated and qualified
No evidence of preexisting medical or physical conditions affecting flight crew
Accident airplane was equipped, dispatched, and maintained in accordance with federal regulations
LaGuardia Airport departure controller’s decision to display only correlated primary radar targets was appropriate
No evidence of preexisting engine, system, or structural failures
Airplane met structural ditching certification regulations in effect at time of certification
Engine met bird-ingestion certification regulations in effect at time of certification
Airframe damage caused by high-energy impact at aft fuselage and forward motion through water
Engines ingested large birds causing mechanical damage preventing sufficient thrust
Electronic control system inability to inform crew of continuing operational status led to wasted time trying to relight engines
Size and number of birds exceeded current bird-ingestion certification standards
Current small/medium flocking bird tests use 100-percent fan speed instead of lowest expected fan speed
Current large flocking bird certification test standards do not require tests on smaller transport-category engines or engine core
Engine design changes and protective screens not viable on turbofan engines like accident engine
Flight crew’s decision to use Engine Dual Failure checklist was in accordance with procedures
Availability of checklist for dual-engine failure at low altitude would have helped crew complete it
Captain started APU, improving outcome by ensuring electrical power and flight envelope protections
Captain’s decision to ditch on Hudson River provided highest probability of survivability
Captain’s difficulty maintaining airspeed resulted in high angles-of-attack, high descent rate, and fuselage damage
Captain’s difficulty maintaining airspeed resulted from high workload, stress, and task saturation
Captain’s decision to use flaps 2 was reasonable and consistent with available guidance
Professionalism and crew resource management contributed to maintaining control and increasing survivability
Comprehensive guidelines on emergency/abnormal checklists would promote standardization
Training pilots for dual-engine failure at low altitude would improve critical thinking and workload management
Better training on visual illusions and touchdown techniques would have prepared crew for ditching
Ditching portion of Engine Dual Failure checklist inconsistent with separate Ditching checklist
Training on sidestick attenuation in alpha-protection mode would improve understanding
Airbus operational procedures review did not evaluate if pilots could attain all ditching parameters
Difficulty attaining Airbus ditching parameters without engine power contributed to fuselage damage
Accident demonstrates bird strike does not need to be typical to be hazardous
Bird strike occurred beyond LGA wildlife hazard responsibilities
Proactive wildlife mitigation approach would provide greater safety benefit
No technological/regulatory changes could lessen probability of similar bird-strike event
Research on aircraft systems may lead to effective bird deterrence methods
Emergency response was timely and efficient due to proximity and training
Flight attendant injured by frame 65 vertical beam
FAA recommended brace positions do not account for seats without breakover feature
Flight attendants initiated evacuation promptly and managed effective evacuation
Airplane equipped for extended overwater operations contributed to lack of fatalities
Determination of cabin safety equipment locations did not consider aft fuselage breaching preventing aft slide/raft use
Passenger immersion protection needs consideration for non-EOW operations
Retrieved life lines could have assisted passengers on wings
Equipping aircraft with flotation seat cushions and life vests on all flights would provide benefits
